37 A potential divider circuit is shown.
150 Ω
12.0 V
5.00 V
R
What is the resistance of resistor R in the potential divider circuit?
A
62.5 Ω
B
107 Ω
C
210 Ω
D
360 Ω

hints: Notice the $12.0 \, \text{V}$ supply is shared between the $150 \, \Omega$ resistor and $R$ in series, with $5.00 \, \text{V}$ shown across $R$ only.
Connect the two voltages using series rules: the voltage across the $150 \, \Omega$ resistor is $12.0 - 5.00 = 7.00 \, \text{V}$, and the same current flows through both resistors.
Set the current through the $150 \, \Omega$ resistor equal to the current through $R$ using $I = V/R$, then rearrange to find $R$.
walkthrough: Identify the series loop: supply $V_{in} = 12.0 \, \text{V}$, top resistor $150 \, \Omega$, bottom resistor $R$, and output $V_{out} = 5.00 \, \text{V}$ across $R$.
Find the voltage across the $150 \, \Omega$ resistor by subtraction: $V_{150} = 12.0 - 5.00 = 7.00 \, \text{V}$.
Use the same series current $I$ in both resistors: $I = V_{150}/150 = 7.00/150 \approx 0.0467 \, \text{A}$.
Apply $R = V_R/I$ for the lower resistor: $R = 5.00/0.0467 \approx 107 \, \Omega$, which also follows from $V_{out} = V_{in}R/(R+150)$.
Check units and size: result is in $\Omega$, and $R < 150 \, \Omega$ as expected because its $5.00 \, \text{V}$ share is smaller than $7.00 \, \text{V}$. This is option B.

A.explanation: Gives $62.5 \, \Omega$ from incorrectly using $5.00 \, \text{V}$ across the $150 \, \Omega$ resistor instead of across $R$.

B.explanation: Matches $R \approx 107 \, \Omega$ from $5.00 = 12.0R/(R+150)$ for the voltage across $R$.

C.explanation: Gives $210 \, \Omega$ from using the $7.00 \, \text{V}$ drop across the $150 \, \Omega$ resistor as if it were across $R$.

D.explanation: Gives $360 \, \Omega$ from inverting the divider ratio to $12.0/5.00$ times $150 \, \Omega$.
